summary: At just 27 people per square mile across more than a thousand square miles, Del Norte is one of the most sparsely populated counties on the entire California coast — a place where old-growth redwoods in Jedediah Smith Redwoods State Park meet wild Pacific shoreline without a single traffic light in between. The housing math is unusually approachable for coastal California: a median home value of $319,600 against a median household income of $66,780 yields a price-to-income ratio under 4.8, a figure that would be almost unrecognizable in the Bay Area or along the Central Coast. But that relative affordability reflects a very thin local job market anchored largely by Pelican Bay State Prison, the county government, and Sutter Coast Hospital — switching employers without a long commute or a career pivot is genuinely difficult. Daily highs average just 61°F year-round, meaning summer heat waves are someone else's problem, but the cool, damp climate and roughly 7.8 hours of daily sunshine also mean gray stretches that test anyone accustomed to Southern California light. The Smith River — the last major undammed river system in the state — offers world-class steelhead fishing minutes from town, and the proximity to Redwood National and State Parks is no exaggeration; trailheads sit practically at the county's doorstep. Crescent City, the only incorporated city, has a small commercial strip with basic grocery and dining options, but variety is limited enough that Brookings, Oregon, twenty miles north, functions as a secondary errand destination. Del Norte essentially trades career optionality and urban convenience for a dramatic, fog-wrapped landscape that most Californians only ever see on a road trip.
